subject: Chemistry
title: Nuclear Fission: Splitting the Atom
description: A fast breakdown of Nuclear Fission: Splitting the Atom for builders.

hook.text: In 1938, Otto Hahn split a uranium atom and released a million times more energy than any chemical reaction.

buildup.text: A neutron strikes uranium-235, making it unstable. The nucleus splits into two smaller atoms plus 2–3 neutrons.

discovery.text: Those freed neutrons hit more uranium atoms, causing a chain reaction. Each split releases enormous energy from E = mc².

twist.text: Lise Meitner actually explained the physics of fission. Hahn got the Nobel Prize alone—one of science's greatest injustices.

climax.text: Controlled fission powers nuclear reactors. Uncontrolled fission is an atomic bomb. Same reaction, different speeds.

punchline.text: Split one atom, free neutrons split more. A chain reaction of pure energy.

quiz.question: What sustains a nuclear fission chain reaction?
options: Neutrons released from each split strike more atoms, causing further splits
Heat from the first split melts surrounding atoms
Electrons escaping from split atoms trigger nearby nuclei

details.summary: Nuclear fission is the process of splitting a heavy atomic nucleus into lighter fragments, releasing enormous energy. Discovered in 1938 by Hahn and Strassmann, fission produces millions of times more energy per atom than any chemical reaction and powers both nuclear reactors and weapons.
details.whyItMatters: Fission provides roughly ten percent of global electricity and reshaped geopolitics through nuclear weapons. It remains central to energy debates about carbon-free power generation.
takeaways: Fission splits heavy nuclei like uranium-235 into lighter elements
Chain reactions occur when released neutrons split more nuclei
One kilogram of uranium yields energy equal to thousands of tons of coal

faq.question: What triggers a nuclear fission chain reaction?
faq.answer: A neutron strikes a fissile nucleus like uranium-235, splitting it and releasing two or three additional neutrons plus energy. Those neutrons strike other nuclei, each releasing more neutrons. If enough fissile material is present, the reaction sustains itself exponentially.

faq.question: Is nuclear fission the same as nuclear fusion?
faq.answer: No. Fission splits heavy atoms; fusion combines light atoms. Both release energy, but through opposite mechanisms. Fission works with heavy elements like uranium; fusion works with light elements like hydrogen. Fusion powers stars; fission powers current nuclear plants.
